docs.title: 3.4. Example 13: The Lifecycle of a Component
3.4.1. A clock
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 13-lifecycle/src/Horloge.tsx - a component that starts and stops
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The life cycle of a component:
//    1. It is AFFICHÉ (mounted): React calls the function and places its
//       result on the page; then it executes its effects (useEffect);
//    2. it is MIS to JOUR, as many times as necessary (its state or
//       props change);
//    3. it is RETIRÉ from the page (removed): React executes the NETTOYAGE of
//       its effects—the function that each effect returned.
// A clock starts a timer (setInterval) when it appears... and
// must stop it when it disappears: otherwise, the timer
// would continue to run for no reason (memory leak).
// =========================================================================

import { useEffect, useEffectEvent, useState } from 'react';

interface Props {
  onJournal: (message: string) => void;
}

export default function Horloge({ onJournal }: Props) {
  const [heure, setHeure] = useState(() => new Date().toLocaleTimeString());

   // useEffectEvent: a function called PAR by an effect, which always reads
   // the most recent props, without being a dependency of the effect. Without
   // it, we would have to include onJournal in the dependencies [...] below,
   // and, since the parent passes a NOUVELLE function on every render, the
   // timer would be stopped and restarted every second
  const journaliser = useEffectEvent((message: string) => onJournal(message));

   // [] : no dependencies. The effect runs UNE times, after the first
   // display; the function it returns runs UNE times when the component is removed
  useEffect(() => {
    journaliser('Horloge : effet - démarrage de la minuterie');
    const minuterie = setInterval(() => setHeure(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()), 1000);
     // the NETTOYAGE
    return () => {
      clearInterval(minuterie);
      journaliser('Horloge : nettoyage - minuterie arrêtée');
    };
  }, []);

  return <div className="display-6 font-monospace">{heure}</div>;
}

The life cycle of a component (lines 4–10): it is mounted (displayed for the first time), updated as many times as necessary, and then unmounted (removed from the page). [React] does not have separate methods for each step: everything goes through [useEffect].

  • Lines 34–42: [useEffect(effet, [])]: With a dependency array VIDE, the effect is executed only once, after the first display. The function it returns (lines 38–41) handles cleanup: [React] executes it when the component is removed from the page (and before each new execution of the effect, when its dependencies change). A clock starts a timer ([setInterval]) on startup... and must stop it ([clearInterval]) when it disappears: otherwise, the timer would continue to run for no reason and attempt to modify the state of a component that no longer exists;
  • Line 30: The effect calls the parent's [onJournal] function. Strictly speaking, it should include it in its dependencies: since the effect uses a prop, it must be re-triggered if the prop changes. However, the parent creates a NOUVELLE function each time it is displayed: the timer would be stopped and restarted continuously. [useEffectEvent] ([React] 19.2) creates a function that always calls the most recent version of [onJournal], without being a dependency of the effect. It is only called from within an effect.

docs.title: 3.4.2. The parent
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 13-lifecycle/src/App.tsx
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
//    - {avecHorloge && <Clock />}: Checking/unchecking the box displays/
//      removes the component (effect, then cleanup; see Horloge.tsx);
//    - useRef: a reference to the <input> element, null until it is
//      displayed; an effect gives it focus as soon as it appears;
//    - an effect that SYNCHRONISE sets the tab title to the input value.
//
// During development, StrictMode (see main.tsx) mounts each component; the
// unmounts it, then remounts it immediately: the log therefore shows startup,
// shutdown, and startup. This is intentional: an effect whose cleanup is poorly written
// (a timer that is never stopped) gives itself away immediately. In production, the
// component is mounted only once.
// =========================================================================

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';
import Horloge from './Horloge';

export default function App() {
  const [avecHorloge, setAvecHorloge] = useState(true);
  const [journal, setJournal] = useState<string[]>([]);
  const [recherche, setRecherche] = useState('');
  const [afficherRecherche, setAfficherRecherche] = useState(false);
  const champ = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

  function tracer(message: string) {
    setJournal((j) => [...j, `${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()} ${message}`]);
  }

   // After the app is first displayed (twice during development: StrictMode)
  useEffect(() => {
    tracer('App : effet du premier affichage');
  }, []);

   // the field has just appeared: we give it focus
  useEffect(() => {
    if (afficherRecherche) {
      champ.current?.focus();
    }
  }, [afficherRecherche]);

   // The tab title updates as you type, right from the start
  useEffect(() => {
    document.title = recherche ? `Recherche : ${recherche}` : 'Exemple 13';
  }, [recherche]);

  return (
    <div className="container py-4" style={{ maxWidth: 720 }}>
      <h1 className="h3 mb-3">Exemple 13 - le cycle de vie d'un composant</h1>

      <div className="card p-3 mb-3">
        <label className="form-check-label mb-2">
          <input type="checkbox" className="form-check-input" checked={avecHorloge}
                 onChange={(e) => setAvecHorloge(e.target.checked)} /> afficher l'horloge
        </label>
        {avecHorloge && <Horloge onJournal={tracer} />}
      </div>

      <div className="card p-3 mb-3">
        {!afficherRecherche ? (
          <button className="btn btn-outline-primary align-self-start" onClick={() => setAfficherRecherche(true)}>Rechercher...</button>
        ) : (
          <input ref={champ} className="form-control" placeholder="le titre de l'onglet suit la saisie" value={recherche}
                 onChange={(e) => setRecherche(e.target.value)} />
        )}
      </div>

      <h2 className="h6">Journal</h2>
      <ol className="small">
        {journal.map((ligne, i) => <li key={i}>{ligne}</li>)}
      </ol>
    </div>
  );
}
  • line 25: a reference to the search field, [null], as long as it is not displayed;
  • lines 32–34: the effect for the first display of [App];
  • lines 37–41: when the field appears, it is given focus: the effect executes APRÈS upon display, when the element exists and the reference points to it;
  • lines 44–46: an effect that synchronizes the tab title with the state;
  • line 57: checking/unchecking the box shows/hides the clock.

Upon startup, the log is surprising: the clock starts, stops, and restarts, and the effect [App] is executed twice. This is [<StrictMode>] (see [main.tsx]): in development only, [React] mounts each component, unmounts it, and then remounts it immediately to verify that its effects can clean up after themselves. A poorly written effect (such as a timer that never stops) is thus immediately revealed: the clock would advance by two seconds at a time. In production, the component is mounted only once. We also note that the effects of the children (the clock) run after those of the parent in AVANT.

Then uncheck and recheck the box, and type “pediatrician” into the search field:

Effects are the most delicate part of [React]. A rule guides their use: an effect synchronizes the component with something outside of [React] (the tab title, a timer, a document event listener, a server). To calculate a value from another, use a variable (Example 02), not an effect. To respond to a user action, use an event handler, not an effect.

docs.title: 3.5. Example 14: Contexts
docs.text: How can you share data and functions between distant components without passing them from props to props through all the intermediaries? With a context. This is how [React] shares what [Angular] stores in its services, which are provided via dependency injection.

docs.title: 3.5.1. A context for the entire application
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 14-contextes/src/contextes/journal.tsx - a context for TOUTE, the application
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// How to share data and functions between components
// remote components, without passing them from props to props through all the
// intermediate components? With a CONTEXTE:
//    1. createContext(valeurParDefaut) creates the context;
//    2. a component FOURNISSEUR, <JournalContexte value={...}>, assigns the
//       value to its descendants, at any depth;
//    3. a descendant of LIT using use(JournalContexte) (or useContext).
// When the provided value changes, all components that read it are
// recalled.
//
// Usage: one file per context, which exports the provider (a
// component that contains the state) and a HOOK to read it (useJournal).
// This is how React shares what Angular organizes into its services.
// =========================================================================

import { createContext, use, useCallback, useMemo, useState, type ReactNode } from 'react';

interface Journal {
  lignes: string[];
  tracer: (message: string) => void;
}

// null: the value read if the AUCUN provider does not encompass the component
const JournalContexte = createContext<Journal | null>(null);

// The provider: it contains the state and passes it down to its descendants
export function JournalFournisseur({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [lignes, setLignes] = useState<string[]>([]);

   // useCallback: the MÊME function varies from one rendering to the next (and is not a
   // new one each time), so that the components that receive it
   // don’t appear to have changed
  const tracer = useCallback((message: string) => {
    setLignes((l) => [`${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()} ${message}`, ...l].slice(0, 6));
  }, []);

   // useMemo: a new object only if the lines have changed
  const valeur = useMemo(() => ({ lignes, tracer }), [lignes, tracer]);

   // React 19: the context itself is the provider component
  return <JournalContexte value={valeur}>{children}</JournalContexte>;
}

// The read hook: a name that starts with "use"
export function useJournal(): Journal {
   // use(context): the value provided by the provider PROCHE
  const journal = use(JournalContexte);
  if (journal === null) {
    throw new Error('useJournal doit être utilisé dans un <JournalFournisseur>');
  }
  return journal;
}
  • lines 21–24: what the context provides: data and a function;
  • line 27: [createContext(valeurParDéfaut)] creates the context. [null]: the value read by a component that is not encompassed by any provider;
  • lines 30–45: the provider: a component that contains the state and passes it to all its descendants, at any depth:
    • line 36: [useCallback(fonction, [dépendances])] passes the MÊME function from one view to the next (as long as the dependencies do not change), rather than creating a new one. Here, there are no dependencies: [setLignes] never changes;
    • line 41: the supplied object is only recreated if [lignes] has changed. Without these precautions, the provider would supply a new object on every display, and all components that read the context would be called unnecessarily;
    • line 44: starting with [React] 19, the context itself is the provider component (previously, we wrote [<JournalContexte.Provider>]);
  • Lines 48–55: a read hook. [use(contexte)] ([React] 19; previously [useContext]) returns the value from the nearest provider. The hook checks to make sure there is one: a clear error is better than an unexpected [null].

docs.title: 3.5.2. A context provided by a component
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 14-contexts/src/contexts/panier.tsx - a context provided by the UN component
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The shopping cart is provided only to a subset of the component tree: those
// encompassed by <PanierFournisseur> (see App.tsx). Two providers placed at
// two different locations on the page would result in two independent shopping carts.
// A provider can itself read other contexts: the shopping cart
// uses the log.
// =========================================================================

import { createContext, use, useMemo, useState, type ReactNode } from 'react';
import { useJournal } from './journal';

export interface Article {
  libelle: string;
  prix: number;
}

interface Panier {
  articles: Article[];
  total: number;
  ajouter: (article: Article) => void;
  retirer: (index: number) => void;
}

const PanierContexte = createContext<Panier | null>(null);

export function PanierFournisseur({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const { tracer } = useJournal();
  const [articles, setArticles] = useState<Article[]>([]);

  const valeur = useMemo<Panier>(
    () => ({
      articles,
      total: articles.reduce((somme, a) => somme + a.prix, 0),
      ajouter: (article) => {
        setArticles((a) => [...a, article]);
        tracer(`panier : + ${article.libelle}`);
      },
      retirer: (index) => {
        tracer(`panier : - ${articles[index].libelle}`);
        setArticles((a) => a.filter((_, i) => i !== index));
      },
    }),
    [articles, tracer],
  );

  return <PanierContexte value={valeur}>{children}</PanierContexte>;
}

export function usePanier(): Panier {
  const panier = use(PanierContexte);
  if (panier === null) {
    throw new Error('usePanier doit être utilisé dans un <PanierFournisseur>');
  }
  return panier;
}

The shopping cart is provided only to a portion of the component tree: those encompassed by [<PanierFournisseur>]. Two providers placed in different locations on the page would result in two independent shopping carts.

  • Line 29: A provider is a component; it can itself read other contexts; the shopping cart uses the log;
  • Lines 32–46: the data ([articles], [total]) and the actions ([ajouter], [retirer]), which are recalculated when the items change.

docs.title: 3.5.3. A configured context
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 14-contexts/src/contexts/horloge.tsx - a context PARAMÉTRÉ
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A clock with a refresh period that is a prop of the
// provider: <HorlogeFournisseur period={5000}>. Two nested providers
// nested: a component reads the one closest to it.
// The clock stops when its provider disappears (effect cleanup).
// =========================================================================

import { createContext, use, useEffect, useState, type ReactNode } from 'react';

// The default value: a fixed date, read by a component without a provider
const HorlogeContexte = createContext<Date>(new Date());

export function HorlogeFournisseur({ periode = 1000, children }: { periode?: number; children: ReactNode }) {
  const [maintenant, setMaintenant] = useState(() => new Date());

   // [periode]: if the parent changes the period, the timer is restarted
  useEffect(() => {
    const minuterie = setInterval(() => setMaintenant(new Date()), periode);
    return () => clearInterval(minuterie);
  }, [periode]);

  return <HorlogeContexte value={maintenant}>{children}</HorlogeContexte>;
}

export function useHorloge(): Date {
  return use(HorlogeContexte);
}
  • line 13: here, a true default value: a fixed date;
  • line 15: the refresh period is a supplier property;
  • lines 19–22: the timer; if the parent changes the period, the effect is cleared and then restarted.

docs.title: 3.5.4. The components
docs.text:
// 14-contextes/src/Catalogue.tsx - a descendant that adds AJOUTE to the cart
import { usePanier, type Article } from './contextes/panier';

const CATALOGUE: Article[] = [
  { libelle: 'Consultation', prix: 30 },
  { libelle: 'Vaccin', prix: 12.5 },
  { libelle: 'Certificat', prix: 5 },
];

export default function Catalogue() {
   // the shopping cart provided by the app (error if none is provided)
  const panier = usePanier();

  return (
    <ul className="list-group">
      {CATALOGUE.map((a) => (
        <li key={a.libelle} className="list-group-item d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center">
          {a.libelle} ({a.prix} €)
          <button className="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" onClick={() => panier.ajouter(a)}>Ajouter</button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

[usePanier()]: the shopping cart provided by a parent (error if no parent provides it).

// =========================================================================
// 14-contextes/src/ResumePanier.tsx
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Another descendant: the MÊME shopping cart that Catalogue (provided by App), but
// SA PROPRE clock, refreshed every 5 seconds. A component does not read
// only the suppliers placed AU-DESSUS by it: ResumePanier therefore places
// a second <HorlogeFournisseur> tag around its content, which it passes to a
// small component, Content.
// =========================================================================

import { HorlogeFournisseur, useHorloge } from './contextes/horloge';
import { usePanier } from './contextes/panier';

function Contenu() {
  const panier = usePanier();
  const maintenant = useHorloge(); // the nearest timer: the 5-second one

  return (
    <div className="card p-3">
      <h2 className="h6">
        Panier ({panier.articles.length} article(s)) - {maintenant.toLocaleTimeString()}
      </h2>
      <ul className="mb-2">
        {panier.articles.map((a, i) => (
          <li key={i}>
            {a.libelle}{' '}
            <button className="btn btn-link btn-sm p-0 align-baseline" onClick={() => panier.retirer(i)}>retirer</button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <strong>Total : {panier.total} €</strong>
    </div>
  );
}

export default function ResumePanier() {
  return (
    <HorlogeFournisseur periode={5000}>
      <Contenu />
    </HorlogeFournisseur>
  );
}
  • lines 14–34: The summary content reads the ET shopping cart and the clock. The closest clock is the 5-second one;
  • lines 36–42: a component reads only the providers placed AU-DESSUS by it: [ResumePanier] therefore places its own [<HorlogeFournisseur periode={5000}>] around a subcomponent, [Contenu].
// =========================================================================
// 14-contexts/src/App.tsx - three levels of contexts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
//    - the log: provided at the very top (main.tsx) to the entire application;
//    - the shopping cart, provided by App: shared by Catalog and ResumePanier,
//      which can access the MÊME shopping cart;
//    - the clock, provided by App (default period, 1 s) ET by
//      ResumePanier (5 s): each has its own.
// =========================================================================

import Catalogue from './Catalogue';
import ResumePanier from './ResumePanier';
import { useJournal } from './contextes/journal';
import { HorlogeFournisseur, useHorloge } from './contextes/horloge';
import { PanierFournisseur } from './contextes/panier';

// the App clock time: a small component, placed at SOUS by the provider
function HeureApp() {
  return <p className="text-muted">Horloge de App : {useHorloge().toLocaleTimeString()}</p>;
}

export default function App() {
  const journal = useJournal();

  return (
    <HorlogeFournisseur>
      <PanierFournisseur>
        <div className="container py-4" style={{ maxWidth: 720 }}>
          <h1 className="h3 mb-3">Exemple 14 - les contextes</h1>
          <HeureApp />
          <div className="row g-3">
            <div className="col-md-6"><Catalogue /></div>
            <div className="col-md-6"><ResumePanier /></div>
          </div>
          <h2 className="h6 mt-3">Journal (contexte racine)</h2>
          <ul className="small">
            {journal.lignes.map((ligne, i) => <li key={i}>{ligne}</li>)}
          </ul>
        </div>
      </PanierFournisseur>
    </HorlogeFournisseur>
  );
}
  • lines 18–20: [App] provides the clock; to read it, a component named SOUS is required, which is supplied by [HeureApp];
  • line 23: [App] reads the log, provided above;
  • Lines 26–27: [App] provides the clock (1 s) and the basket to its descendants.

And the provider of the log, placed at the very top:

// =========================================================================
// 14-contextes/src/main.tsx - the log provider includes App: it
// is therefore available in TOUTE the app
// =========================================================================

import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css';
import App from './App';
import { JournalFournisseur } from './contextes/journal';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <JournalFournisseur>
      <App />
    </JournalFournisseur>
  </StrictMode>,
);

The clock for [App] advances every second, while the shopping cart’s clock advances every five seconds. Both components see the same shopping cart, and the log records every addition.

A context is sufficient for data that rarely changes (the logged-in user, the language, a theme) or that applies only to part of the page. When a state is shared across the entire application and changes frequently, a “store” is preferred (Example 20).

docs.title: 3.6. Example 15: Writing Your Own Hooks
docs.text: A component reuses the view; a custom hook reuses a behavior, along with its state. It is a function whose name begins with [use], and which itself calls hooks. This example writes two of them, for the two behaviors that Example 15 of the [Angular] course assigned to directives.

docs.title: 3.6.1. Highlight an element on hover
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 15-custom-hooks/src/hooks/useSurvol.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A HOOK PERSONNALISÉ is a function whose name begins with "use," and
// which itself calls hooks (useState, useEffect, useRef...). It
// allows a COMPORTEMENT (along with its state) to be reused in multiple
// components, just as a component reuses the display.
//
// This one highlights an element when the mouse hovers over it. It returns the attributes to be applied
// on the element: <li {...useSurvol('#d1e7dd')}>. Each call has its
// own state: two highlighted elements do not interfere with each other.
// =========================================================================

import { useState } from 'react';

export function useSurvol(couleur = '#fff3cd') {
  const [survole, setSurvole] = useState(false);
  return {
    style: { backgroundColor: survole ? couleur : undefined, transition: 'background-color 0.2s' },
    onMouseEnter: () => setSurvole(true),
    onMouseLeave: () => setSurvole(false),
  };
}

The hook has its own state ([survole]) and returns the attributes to be applied to the element: a style and two event handlers. Each component that calls it has its own state: two highlighted elements do not interfere with each other.

docs.title: 3.6.2. Long click
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 15-custom-hooks/src/hooks/useClicLong.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
//      const clicLong = useClicLong(() => delete(m), 1000);
//      <button {...clicLong.gestionnaires} className={clicLong.enCours ? 'pressed' : ''}>
// The action is executed only if the button is held down for one
// second: protection against accidental clicks. enCours indicates whether a
// press is in progress (to display it).
// The timer is stopped if the component disappears while the button is being pressed.
// =========================================================================

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';

export function useClicLong(action: () => void, duree = 1000) {
  const [enCours, setEnCours] = useState(false);
   // A value that persists across SANS displays: useRef
  const minuterie = useRef<number | undefined>(undefined);

   // When the component is removed: no orphaned timer
  useEffect(() => () => clearTimeout(minuterie.current), []);

  function commencer() {
    setEnCours(true);
    minuterie.current = window.setTimeout(() => {
      setEnCours(false);
      action();
    }, duree);
  }

  function arreter() {
    clearTimeout(minuterie.current);
    setEnCours(false);
  }

  return {
    enCours,
    gestionnaires: { onPointerDown: commencer, onPointerUp: arreter, onPointerLeave: arreter },
  };
}
  • line 17: the timer’s identifier—a value that must persist across views but isn’t displayed—a reference;
  • line 20: an effect with no action, which simply cleans up: if the component disappears while the button is held down, the timer is stopped;
  • lines 22–28: the action is executed only if the button is held down for one second: a safeguard against accidental clicks;
  • lines 35–38: the hook returns the state ([enCours], to display it) and the pointer event handlers (mouse, finger, or stylus).

docs.title: 3.6.3. Give focus
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 15-custom-hooks/src/hooks/autofocus.ts - a "ref callback"
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// ref={function}: React calls the function with the HTML element as soon as it
// is rendered on the page (and, in React 19, calls the function that
// may return when it is removed). This is not a hook:
// just a simple function that can be reused anywhere:
//      <input ref={autofocus} />
// (React also supports the autoFocus attribute, which does the same thing.)
// =========================================================================

export function autofocus(element: HTMLElement | null): void {
  element?.focus();
}

A ref callback: you can assign a function to the [ref] attribute, which [React] calls with the HTML element as soon as it is placed on the page. This is not a hook, but a simple function.

docs.title: 3.6.4. Usage
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 15-custom-hooks/src/App.tsx - reusing behaviors
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Hooks are only called at the PREMIER NIVEAU of a component (never inside
// a loop, a condition, or a nested function): React
// by their ORDRE call site. To achieve per-line behavior for a
// list, you therefore write one small component per line, which calls its hooks.
// =========================================================================

import { useState } from 'react';
import { useSurvol } from './hooks/useSurvol';
import { useClicLong } from './hooks/useClicLong';
import { autofocus } from './hooks/autofocus';

// the button’s style during a long press
const styleAppui = { outline: '4px solid #dc3545' };

// a row in the list: it calls SES hooks
function LigneMedecin({ nom, pair, onSupprimer }: { nom: string; pair: boolean; onSupprimer: () => void }) {
   // every other line: the default color; the others, green
  const survol = useSurvol(pair ? undefined : '#d1e7dd');
  const clicLong = useClicLong(onSupprimer, 1000);

  return (
    <li className="list-group-item d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center" {...survol}>
      {nom}
      <button className="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger" style={clicLong.enCours ? styleAppui : undefined}
              {...clicLong.gestionnaires}>
        Supprimer (appui long)
      </button>
    </li>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  const [medecins, setMedecins] = useState(['Mme Marie PELISSIER', 'Mr Paul TATOU', 'Melle Sophie DUPONT']);
  const [message, setMessage] = useState('');

  function supprimer(nom: string) {
    setMedecins((m) => m.filter((x) => x !== nom));
    setMessage(`${nom} a été supprimé.`);
  }

  return (
    <div className="container py-4" style={{ maxWidth: 640 }}>
      <h1 className="h3 mb-3">Exemple 15 - écrire ses propres hooks</h1>
      <input ref={autofocus} className="form-control mb-3" placeholder="ce champ a reçu le focus tout seul" />

      <p className="small text-muted">Survolez les lignes ; maintenez un bouton enfoncé une seconde pour supprimer.</p>
      <ul className="list-group mb-3">
        {medecins.map((m, i) => (
          <LigneMedecin key={m} nom={m} pair={i % 2 === 0} onSupprimer={() => supprimer(m)} />
        ))}
      </ul>
      {message && <p className="alert alert-info">{message}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

Hooks follow a strict rule: they are called only at the top level of a component or another hook, never within a loop, a condition, or a nested function. [React] identifies each [useState] by its call order: if the order changed from one display to another, the states would become mixed up.

  • Lines 19–33: For line-by-line behavior in a list, you cannot call the hooks directly in [map]; instead, write a small component for each line that calls the SES hooks;
  • Line 25: The tooltip attributes, spread across the line;
  • line 28: the long-press handlers for the button and its style while pressed;
  • line 47: the callback reference;
  • Line 52: one line per doctor.

Upon startup, the field has focus. While holding down the second button:

Then, once a second has elapsed:

Custom hooks are the primary way to reuse code in [React]. The libraries provide many of them: [useForm] (example 08), [useNavigate] (example 17), [useTranslation] (example 21), [useQuery] (example 24)...

docs.title: 3.7. Example 16: A reusable confirmation window
docs.text: “Are you sure?”: [window.confirm()] exists, but its buttons cannot be formatted or translated. It is replaced by a [Bootstrap] window, controlled by a context.

docs.title: 3.7.1. The context
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 16-confirmation/src/confirmation/confirmation.tsx
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// “Are you sure?”: window.confirm() exists, but we can neither
// style it nor translate its buttons. We replace it with a window
// Bootstrap dialog, controlled by a context (see Example 14).
//
// Tip: confirm(message) returns a PROMESSE, which evaluates to true (Yes)
// or false (No) when the user responds. The calling code is written
// just as simply as with window.confirm:
//
//      const confirm = useConfirmation();
//      if (await confirm('Delete this doctor?')) { ... }
//
// The provider displays the window itself: simply place it
// time around the entire application (see main.tsx).
// =========================================================================

import { createContext, use, useCallback, useRef, useState, type ReactNode } from 'react';
import FenetreConfirmation from './FenetreConfirmation';

type Confirmer = (message: string) => Promise<boolean>;

const ConfirmationContexte = createContext<Confirmer | null>(null);

export function ConfirmationFournisseur({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [message, setMessage] = useState<string | null>(null); // null: window closed
   // the function that will resolve the current promise: it is not displayed,
   // so it is a reference and not a state
  const repondre = useRef<((oui: boolean) => void) | null>(null);

  const confirmer = useCallback<Confirmer>((texte) => {
    repondre.current?.(false); // Is there still an open question? It is set to "no"
    setMessage(texte);
    return new Promise<boolean>((resolve) => {
      repondre.current = resolve;
    });
  }, []);

  function reponse(oui: boolean) {
    setMessage(null);
    const r = repondre.current;
    repondre.current = null;
    r?.(oui);
  }

  return (
    <ConfirmationContexte value={confirmer}>
      {children}
      {message !== null && <FenetreConfirmation message={message} onReponse={reponse} />}
    </ConfirmationContexte>
  );
}

export function useConfirmation(): Confirmer {
  const confirmer = use(ConfirmationContexte);
  if (confirmer === null) {
    throw new Error('useConfirmation doit être utilisé dans un <ConfirmationFournisseur>');
  }
  return confirmer;
}

Tip: [confirmer(message)] returns a promise, which resolves to [true] (Yes) or [false] (No) when the user responds. The calling code is then just as simple as with [window.confirm]: [if (await confirmer('Supprimer ce médecin ?')) {...}].

  • Line 22: what the context provides: a function;
  • line 27: the message displayed; [null]: the window is closed;
  • line 30: the function that will resolve the current promise. It is not displayed: it is a reference, not a state;
  • Lines 32–38: Open the window and return a promise whose function is retained as [resolve]. An unanswered question is treated as “no”;
  • lines 40–45: the response: close the window and resolve the promise;
  • line 50: the provider displays the window itself when there is a question.

docs.title: 3.7.2. The window
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 16-confirmation/src/confirmation/FenetreConfirmation.tsx
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The modal window:
//    - Same Bootstrap classes as a real modal (.modal, .modal-backdrop),
//      displayed "hard-coded" (show d-block): no need for the JavaScript from
//      Bootstrap;
//    - createPortal: the window is placed at the end of <body>, not where
//      the component is written. It thus bypasses the styles of its
//      ancestors (overflow, z-index...), while remaining a standard React
//      (props, events);
//    - keyboard: Esc = No; focus is placed on the "No" button (the
//      least risky choice) upon opening.
// =========================================================================

import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { createPortal } from 'react-dom';

interface Props {
  message: string;
  onReponse: (oui: boolean) => void;
}

export default function FenetreConfirmation({ message, onReponse }: Props) {
   // Esc, anywhere on the page: a listener attached to the DOCUMENT
   // upon opening, removed upon closing (clearing the effect)
  useEffect(() => {
    const clavier = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
      if (e.key === 'Escape') onReponse(false);
    };
    document.addEventListener('keydown', clavier);
    return () => document.removeEventListener('keydown', clavier);
  }, [onReponse]);

  return createPortal(
    <>
      <div className="modal-backdrop fade show"></div>
      {/* A click on the background (not inside the window) counts as “no” */}
      <div className="modal fade show d-block" tabIndex={-1} role="alertdialog" aria-modal="true"
           onClick={(e) => e.target === e.currentTarget && onReponse(false)}>
        <div className="modal-dialog modal-dialog-centered">
          <div className="modal-content">
            <div className="modal-header">
              <h5 className="modal-title">Confirmation</h5>
              <button type="button" className="btn-close" aria-label="Fermer" onClick={() => onReponse(false)}></button>
            </div>
            <div className="modal-body">
              <p className="mb-0">{message}</p>
            </div>
            <div className="modal-footer">
              {/* autoFocus: React gives focus to this button when it appears */}
              <button type="button" className="btn btn-secondary" autoFocus onClick={() => onReponse(false)}>Non, revenir</button>
              <button type="button" className="btn btn-danger" onClick={() => onReponse(true)}>Oui, confirmer</button>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </>,
    document.body,
  );
}
  • lines 27–33: the Esc key, anywhere on the page: a listener attached to DOCUMENT when the window opens, and removed when it closes (cleanup). This is typically the job of an effect: connecting to something external to [React];
  • line 35: [createPortal(jsx, élément)] displays JSX somewhere other than where the component is written: here, at the end of [<body>]. The window thus bypasses the styles of its ancestors ([overflow], [z-index]...), while remaining an ordinary [React] component (props, events);
  • lines 37–39: the [Bootstrap] classes of a true modal window, hard-coded ([show d-block]): no need for the [JavaScript] from [Bootstrap];
  • line 40: a click on the background (not inside the window) counts as “No”;
  • line 52: [React] gives focus to the “No” button—the safest choice—when it appears.

docs.title: 3.7.3. Usage
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 16-confirmation/src/App.tsx - use the confirmation window
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Same page as Example 21 from the course NestJS (links, buttons, confirmation),
// but without any round trips to a server.
// =========================================================================

import { useState } from 'react';
import { useConfirmation } from './confirmation/confirmation';

interface Contact {
  id: number;
  nom: string;
}

export default function App() {
  const confirmer = useConfirmation();
  const [contacts, setContacts] = useState<Contact[]>([
    { id: 1, nom: 'Jean MARTIN' },
    { id: 2, nom: 'Alice DURAND' },
    { id: 3, nom: 'Luc GERMAN' },
  ]);
  const [message, setMessage] = useState('');

   // An async function: it “waits” for the user’s response
  async function supprimer(c: Contact) {
    if (!(await confirmer(`Supprimer le contact ${c.nom} ?`))) {
      setMessage('Suppression abandonnée.');
      return;
    }
    setContacts((liste) => liste.filter((x) => x.id !== c.id));
    setMessage(`${c.nom} a été supprimé.`);
  }

  async function toutSupprimer() {
    if (await confirmer(`Supprimer les ${contacts.length} contacts ?`)) {
      setContacts([]);
      setMessage('Tous les contacts ont été supprimés.');
    }
  }

  return (
    <div className="container py-4" style={{ maxWidth: 640 }}>
      <h1 className="h3 mb-3">Exemple 16 - une fenêtre de confirmation</h1>
      <ul className="list-group mb-3">
        {contacts.map((c) => (
          <li key={c.id} className="list-group-item d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center">
            {c.nom}
            <button className="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger" onClick={() => supprimer(c)}>Supprimer</button>
          </li>
        ))}
        {contacts.length === 0 && <li className="list-group-item text-muted">Aucun contact.</li>}
      </ul>
      <button className="btn btn-danger" disabled={contacts.length === 0} onClick={toutSupprimer}>Tout supprimer</button>
      {message && <p className="alert alert-info mt-3">{message}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}
  • line 17: the confirmation function;
  • lines 26–33: a function [async]: it “waits” ([await]) for the user’s response without blocking the page.
import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css';
import App from './App';
import { ConfirmationFournisseur } from './confirmation/confirmation';

// the confirmation window, UNE once for the entire application
createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <ConfirmationFournisseur>
      <App />
    </ConfirmationFournisseur>
  </StrictMode>,
);

The window, UNE, is used once for the entire application: its provider includes [App].

docs.title: 12. Conclusion
docs.text:
We wrote the client [React] for the application [RdvMedecins]. For the user, it displays the same pages as the HTML application from the [NestJS] course, and as the [Vue.js] and [Angular] clients from previous courses; For the developer, everything has changed:

  • the server no longer generates pages. It exposes a API JSON, whose contract (routes, body, codes, and error keys) was sufficient to write the client without ever reading its code. The server is, in fact, exactly the same as that of the [Vue.js] and [Angular] clients: only its comments have changed;
  • the pages, language, formatting, messages, and navigation have shifted within the browser;
  • As for security, nothing has changed: it is still the server that authenticates (cookie [HttpOnly]), verifies roles and management rules, and decides what a patient is authorized to view. The client simply displays whatever the server sends it.

Readers who have followed the three lessons can compare the three frameworks on the same application:

  • [React] is more of a display library than a full-fledged framework: it consists of components—which are functions—from JSX, and hooks. For the rest, we had to make some choices: [React Router] for the pages, [TanStack Query] for server data, [Zustand] for shared state, [i18next] for languages, and [Vite] for building. This flexibility comes at a cost: two [React] applications may not resemble each other at all;
  • [Angular], on the other hand, provides everything (router, forms, HTTP client, interceptors, build tools), along with a recommended way to use them: more code and concepts (classes, decorators, dependency injection, observables), but applications that all look alike;
  • [Vue.js] falls somewhere in between: an official router and store, with templates similar to those in HTML;
  • Finally, responsiveness differs. [Vue.js] and [Angular] track signals: when a value changes, only what depends on it is updated. [React] re-renders the component whose state has changed, then compares the result to the previous one: this is easier to understand (a component is a function of its props and state), but it’s up to the developer to declare the dependencies of the effects and to stabilize certain values ([useCallback], the keys in [key]). The [React] compiler ([React Compiler]), which can be added to the project, performs this stabilization automatically.

The [React] concepts covered in this course (components, props, state, effects, custom hooks, contexts, form actions, [Suspense]) are those found in any modern [React] application. To learn more:

  • the official documentation, https://react.dev, and its tutorials;
  • tests: [Vitest] and [Testing Library] for unit tests of components and hooks, [Playwright] for end-to-end tests (this is the one used to generate the screenshots in this document);
  • server-side rendering: the “framework” mode of [React Router] or [Next.js] generates the first page on the server, and the server components of [React] read the data directly from there: this would then partially mirror the architecture of the course [NestJS];
  • the course “An Example of a React Client/Server: NestJS” (2026), which examines both a [React] client and its server.

docs.title: 11. Deployment
docs.text:
In development, two servers work together: the [Vite] development server (the client) and the JSON server (the API). In production, there is only one:

1. Build the client. In the [rdvmedecins-react] folder:

npm run build

The console displays:

> rdvmedecins-react@1.0.0 build
> tsc --noEmit && vite build

vite v8.3.1 building client environment for production...
transforming...
✓ 205 modules transformed.
rendering chunks...
computing gzip size...
dist/index.html                               1.14 kB │ gzip:   0.60 kB
dist/assets/index-CMDWaW-Y.css                0.49 kB │ gzip:   0.29 kB
dist/assets/bibliotheques-CqLr8KVv.css      230.06 kB │ gzip:  30.68 kB
dist/assets/personnes.config-CwIZX_RT.js      0.54 kB │ gzip:   0.26 kB
dist/assets/rolldown-runtime-CbXtAM7H.js      0.58 kB │ gzip:   0.36 kB
dist/assets/ChampsPersonne-Ci3eLvgx.js        1.68 kB │ gzip:   0.71 kB
dist/assets/Personnes-Cnfa5bDw.js             2.03 kB │ gzip:   0.83 kB
dist/assets/EspacePatient-CJaqGM9p.js         2.38 kB │ gzip:   0.98 kB
dist/assets/Inscription-CsY1sB3V.js           2.47 kB │ gzip:   1.09 kB
dist/assets/PersonneFormulaire-DkPyjstx.js    2.85 kB │ gzip:   1.35 kB
dist/assets/MonCompte-C14hUh6b.js             3.86 kB │ gzip:   1.39 kB
dist/assets/index-C7BOzjUE.js                38.38 kB │ gzip:  12.16 kB
dist/assets/bibliotheques-B3ai-pW0.js       394.23 kB │ gzip: 123.37 kB

✓ built in 565ms

First, [tsc --noEmit] checks the types for the entire project: [Vite] does not do this; it simply removes the syntax from [TypeScript]. A type error stops the build. Then [Vite] builds the entire application in the [dist/] folder: a [index.html] page, style sheets, and optimized [JavaScript] files:

  • [bibliotheques-....js]: the library code ([React], [React Router], [TanStack Query], [i18next]...), stored in a separate file by the configuration of [vite.config.ts]. It rarely changes: from one version of the application to the next, the browser keeps it in the cache. [bibliotheques-....css]: the stylesheet for [Bootstrap];
  • [index-....js]: NOTRE code, used for pages loaded immediately (login, calendar) and the rest of the application;
  • Each page loaded on demand ([lazy], see [routes.tsx]) has its own file ([MonCompte-....js]...), downloaded on the first visit; [ChampsPersonne-....js] and [personnes.config-....js] contain code common to several of these pages;
  • Upon startup, the browser downloads approximately 170 KB once compressed by the server (gzip column), of which 150 KB is for libraries;
  • Each file’s name contains a hash of its contents ([index-C7BOzjUE.js]): a new version will have a different name, and a browser will never be able to cache an outdated version. Only [index.html] retains its name: it is this file that references the others.

You can try the version built with [npm run preview] (http://localhost:4173, using the same proxy to the JSON server).

2. Upload it to the server. Copy the CONTENU file from the [dist/] folder into a [client/] folder at the root of the JSON server ([rdvmedecins-nestjs-json/client/index.html], [rdvmedecins-nestjs-json/client/assets/...]), then restart the server. It displays:

[Nest] LOG [RdvMedecins] client React servi depuis .../rdvmedecins-nestjs-json/client
[Nest] LOG [RdvMedecins] serveur JSON démarré : http://localhost:8080/api

The complete application is now available at http://localhost:8080. The server serves the client’s files and returns [index.html] for any other URL outside of /api: reloading the /agenda page works (it is the client’s browser that displays it). For the curious reader, it is the [src/web/client-spa.ts] file on the server that performs this task.

3. In a real production environment, don’t forget the file [.env] on the server:

  • a long, random [JWT_SECRET];
  • an empty [CAPTCHA_TEST];
  • [COOKIE_SECURE=true] if the site is served via HTTPS (it must be: passwords are being transmitted);
  • [TRUST_PROXY=true] if the server is behind a proxy ([nginx]...), so that the attempt limit sees the clients’ actual IP address.

We then launch the compiled server: [npm run build], followed by [npm run start:prod].

docs.title: 2.1. Example 01: The Structure of a React Application
2.1.1. The package.json file
docs.text:
The file [package.json] in the examples folder declares the libraries used and the project commands:

{
  "name": "exemples-react",
  "private": true,
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "vite --config vite.config.ts",
    "build": "vite build --config vite.config.ts",
    "check": "tsc --noEmit"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "@tanstack/react-query": "^5.104.0",
    "bootstrap": "^5.3.8",
    "i18next": "^26.4.2",
    "react": "^19.3.0",
    "react-dom": "^19.3.0",
    "react-hook-form": "^7.89.0",
    "react-i18next": "^17.0.15",
    "react-router": "^8.4.0",
    "zustand": "^5.0.15"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@types/react": "^19.2.18",
    "@types/react-dom": "^19.2.7",
    "@vitejs/plugin-react": "^6.1.1",
    "typescript": "~6.0.2",
    "vite": "^8.3.0"
  }
}

Let’s break down this file:

  • Line 5: The [JavaScript] files in the project are ES modules ([import] / [export]), which is the current language standard;
  • Lines 6–10: The project commands, launched by [npm run <nom>] (or [npm start] for the [start] command):
    • [npm start 05-champs-controles] launches [vite --config vite.config.ts 05-champs-controles]: the development server for Example 05;
    • [npm run build 05-champs-controles] launches [vite build ...]: the production version of Example 05, located in the [05-champs-controles/dist/] folder;
    • [npm run check] launches the compiler [TypeScript] ([tsc]), which checks the types of the examples in TOUS without producing anything ([--noEmit]);
  • lines 11–21: the libraries the application needs in the browser: [react] (the core: components, state, hooks) and [react-dom] (display on a web page), [react-router] (the router, examples 17 and 18), [react-hook-form] (example 08), [zustand] (example 20), [i18next] and [react-i18next] (languages, example 21), [@tanstack/react-query] (reading data from the server, example 24), and [Bootstrap] for formatting;
  • Lines 22–28: Development tools: [Vite] ([vite]), its plugin for [React] ([@vitejs/plugin-react]), the [TypeScript] compiler, and the type descriptions from [React] for [TypeScript] ([@types/react], [@types/react-dom]). They are not part of the application delivered to users.

The prefix [^] for a version ([^19.3.0]) allows [npm] to install a newer version of the same major version (19.x.y); the prefix [~] ([~6.0.2]) allows only hotfixes (6.0.x).

In a standard project, this file is created by the [npm create vite@latest nom-du-projet -- --template react-ts] command, which generates a complete, ready-to-run [React] application. The examples in this course were written by hand so that twenty-five of them could be included in a single folder.

docs.title: 2.1.2. The file vite.config.ts
docs.text:
[Vite] is the recommended build tool for a [React] application: a very fast development server and a production compiler. Its configuration, common to all examples:

// =========================================================================
// vite.config.ts - the Vite configuration, common to all examples
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Vite is React’s build tool: a development server
// (npm start) and a production compiler (npm run build). Each
// example is a folder with its own page index.html; you give it a
// name to Vite, which makes it the RACINE (root) of the application:
//
//      npm start 05-champs-contro     les  -> vite --config vite.config.ts 05-champs-controles
//      npm run build 05-champs-contro les  -> the result in 05-champs-controles/dist/
// =========================================================================

import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

export default defineConfig({
   // the React plugin: the JSX syntax, and "hot" reloading (a
   // code change updates the page without losing the displayed state)
  plugins: [react()],
  server: {
    port: 5173,
     // PROXY: any browser request to /api/... is forwarded
     // to the server JSON RdvMedecins (port 8080). It is only used starting from
     // Example 22 (see the chapter “Communicating with the Server”).
    proxy: {
       '/api': 'http://localhost:8080',
    },
  },
});
  • lines 9–10 (comment): the name of the example, provided to the command, becomes the root ([root]) of the application: [Vite] searches for the page [index.html] and the folder [public/], and stores the result of the build ([dist/]) there;
  • line 19: the [React] plugin: it compiles the JSX syntax (see below) and enables hot reloading: a change to a component’s code is applied to the page without reloading it, preserving the displayed state as much as possible;
  • line 21: the development server port;
  • lines 25–27: the proxy, which will only be used starting with Example 22: any request from the browser to an address beginning with [/api] is forwarded to the server JSON [RdvMedecins]. We’ll come back to this later.

docs.title: 2.1.3. The tsconfig.json file
docs.text:
The [TypeScript] configuration common to all examples:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2023",
    "lib": ["ES2023", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"],
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "types": ["vite/client"],
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "strict": true,
    "noUnusedLocals": true,
    "noUnusedParameters": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "noEmit": true
  },
  "include": ["*/src", "commun", "vite.config.ts"]
}
  • lines 3–6: modern [JavaScript] code (ES2023), browser definitions ([DOM]), and modules resolved as done by the build tool;
  • line 7: definitions specific to [Vite] (for example, importing a stylesheet, [import './App.css'], is allowed);
  • line 8: the JSX syntax is accepted and compiled for [React];
  • Lines 9–13: the strict mode of [TypeScript] (strictly checked types, including [null] and [undefined]), and additional checks: an unused variable or parameter is reported as an error;
  • line 14: an import that applies only to types is written as [import type { ... }] (or [import { type X }]): this tells the build tool that it no longer exists in the generated [JavaScript] file;
  • line 16: a file named JSON can be imported as a module (Example 21);
  • line 18: [tsc] only checks the types; it is [Vite] that actually compiles the code (it simply removes the types without checking them: hence the command [npm run check]);
  • line 20: the files that are checked: those from all the examples.

The [VS Code] editor uses this configuration: a typo in a component ([{titr}] instead of [{titre}]) is underlined in red as soon as it is typed.

docs.title: 2.1.4. The page index.html
docs.text:
Each example has its own page, HTML. The page for Example 01:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Exemple 01 - une première application</title>
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
</head>
<body>
   <!-- the React application is displayed in this element (see src/main.tsx) -->
  <div id="root"></div>
   <!-- the entry point: a JavaScript module, compiled on the fly by Vite -->
  <script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx"></script>
</body>
</html>

This is the only page the browser will load. It is almost empty:

  • line 10: the element in which [React] will display the application;
  • line 12: the application’s entry point, a [TypeScript] module. The browser does not understand [TypeScript]: it is [Vite] that compiles this file—and the files it imports—when the browser requests them.

There are no [<link>] tags here: the style sheets are imported by the code (see [main.tsx]), and [Vite] adds them to the page itself.

docs.title: 2.1.5. The entry point: main.tsx
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 01-first-app/src/main.tsx - the application's entry point
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// index.html loads this file. It starts the React application:
//    1. createRoot (element): React takes control of the <div id="root">
//       on the page;
//    2. root.render(<App />): it renders the RACINE component, App, within it.
// Style sheets are modules just like any other: they are imported.
// =========================================================================

import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css';
import App from './App';

// The "!" tells TypeScript: this element exists (it is in index.html)
createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
   // StrictMode: In development mode only, React performs additional checks
   // additional checks (see Example 13). It does not display anything on its own.
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>,
);

A [.tsx] file is a [TypeScript] file that contains JSX.

  • Line 12: the function from [react-dom] that launches an application within a web page;
  • line 13: the stylesheet for [Bootstrap]: an unnamed import, used solely to add it to the page;
  • Line 14: the root component of the application, the function exported by [App.tsx];
  • line 17: [React] takes ownership of the [<div id="root">] element. [document.getElementById('root')] can return [null] for [TypeScript]: [!] asserts that it exists;
  • lines 20–22: [render(...)] displays the component [App] within this element. [<App />] is part of JSX: the use of the [App] component as a tag. [<StrictMode>] is a component of [React], which does not display anything itself but enables additional checks during development (example 13).

docs.title: 2.1.6. The root components: App.tsx and App.css
docs.text:
A component named [React] is a function:

// =========================================================================
// 01-first-app/src/App.tsx - a first component
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A React component is a FONCTION, whose name begins with an
// uppercase letter, which RENVOIE determines what to display, written in JSX: from HTML
// in the code TypeScript. React calls this function to generate the
// page; it calls RAPPELLE every time the component’s state changes, and uses
// updates the page with the new result.
// =========================================================================

import { useState } from 'react';
// a stylesheet, imported by the component that uses it
import './App.css';

// "ordinary" data, outside the component: it never changes
const titre = 'Bienvenue dans React';
const langages = ['TypeScript', 'HTML', 'CSS'];

export default function App() {
   // useState(0): a data item from ÉTAT, with an initial value of 0. We receive its
   // value ACTUELLE (counter) and the function that changes it (setCompteur).
   // Calling setCompteur instructs React to RAPPELER App to update
   // the page. You should never modify the page yourself.
  const [compteur, setCompteur] = useState(0);
  const [heure, setHeure] = useState(() => new Date().toLocaleTimeString());

   // a function called by the button
  function incrementer() {
    setCompteur((n) => n + 1);
    setHeure(new Date().toLocaleTimeString());
  }

   // the JSX returned: { expression } inserts the value of an expression;
   // className replaces the HTML class attribute (a reserved word in JavaScript)
  return (
    <div className="container py-4">
      <h1 className="h3">{titre}</h1>
      <p>Cette page est fabriquée dans le navigateur, par React, à partir de index.html, main.tsx et du composant App.</p>
      <p>
        On y écrit du {langages.join(', ')} ({langages.length} langages).
      </p>

      {/* onClick: the function to call when clicked (see example 04) */}
      <button className="btn btn-primary" onClick={incrementer}>
        Cliquez-moi
      </button>
      <p className="mt-3 compteur">
        Vous avez cliqué {compteur} fois (dernier clic : {heure}).
      </p>
    </div>
  );
}
  • Line 11: the hook [useState], provided by [React];
  • line 13: the component’s style sheet;
  • lines 16–17: two ordinary data items, declared outside the component: they never change;
  • line 19: the component: a function whose name begins with a capital letter (this is how JSX distinguishes a component, [<App />], from an element, HTML, [<div>]). [export default]: this is what the module exports by default, imported into [main.tsx] by [import App from './App'];
  • Line 24: [useState(0)] creates a state variable with an initial value of 0. It returns an array of two elements, which we “unpack”: the current value ([compteur]) and the function that changes it ([setCompteur]). The state is stored by [React]: it persists from one function call to the next;
  • Line 25: You can assign a function to [useState] that calculates the initial value; it is called only the first time the page is displayed;
  • Lines 28–30: A function called by the button. It does not modify the page; it changes the state. [setCompteur((n) => n + 1)] calculates the new value based on the old one. Each call to the function [setXxx] instructs [React] to call [App]; [React] compares the new result to the old one and updates only the parts of the page that have changed;
  • lines 35–51: the returned JSX, i.e., what should be displayed:
    • the JSX resembles the HTML, with a few differences: the attribute [class] is written as [className] ([class] is a reserved word for [JavaScript]), each tag must be closed ([<br />], [<input />]), and the entire structure must have UN as its root element;
    • Line 37: [{ expression }] inserts the value of an expression [TypeScript]. It is escaped: if [titre] contained [<b>], [<b>] would be displayed without the tag being interpreted;
    • line 40: the expression can be anything: a method call, a calculation;
    • line 43: a comment in JSX is written as [{/* ... */}];
    • line 44: Clicking the button calls the function [incrementer] (see Example 04). The function itself is provided without parentheses: [onClick={incrementer()}] would call it immediately, while it is being displayed;
    • line 48: the current value of the state. When the state changes, [App] is called again, and this text changes.

JSX is not the same as HTML: it is a convenient notation for function calls. The compiler transforms [<h1 className="h3">{titre}</h1>] into a call of the form [jsx('h1', { className: 'h3', children: titre })], which creates an object describing the element. The component therefore returns a tree of objects (the “virtual DOM”), which [React] compares to the previous tree to determine what to change in the actual page.

And its style sheet:

/* a stylesheet imported by App.tsx; ATTENTION: it is applied
   à toute la page, et non au seul composant App (cf. exemple 10) */
.compteur {
  font-weight: bold;
  color: #087ea4;
}

Unlike [Angular] or [Vue.js], [React] does not isolate a component’s styles: an imported stylesheet applies to the entire page. Example 10 will demonstrate the “CSS modules,” which restrict a class to a single component.
